My finding
CASE 9 · YEAR 6

The three witness cards are Edmund Barton, Rose Scott, and Mei Quong Tart. Further questions — including who
could vote in the referendums, section 127, the 1902 Franchise Act, and what “us all” included — are in Super
Sleuths.

There is no answer at the back. The records show that some people had a vote, and that some
people were written out of the count and out of the roll. They do not capture every voice that
was never asked. Write only what these records can support. Do not invent what they do not
say.

Who had a say in making the nation, and who was left out?
Circle one: Everyone who lived here had a say · Some people voted, and some were written out of
the Constitution and the roll · The speeches tell the whole story · We can’t know, from this file,
whose voices were never written down · Another finding, written below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
The speeches still tell us who was meant by “us all.” The Constitution, and the Franchise Act
that followed, still show who was counted, who could vote, and who was left out. Section 127,
and the wording of the race power, were later changed, in 1967. The franchise later widened.
Those changes matter, and they do not close the file. The question of who gets a say in the
nation is not only a question about 1901.

  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The Herald’s Parkes, not a rewritten “I”
  The typographic page follows The Sydney Morning Herald of 25 October 1889, p. 8. The speech was
  given on 24 October. The Herald mostly used reported speech: “the great question which they had to
  consider was…” Later retellings, including some museum pages, turn this into first person (“we have
  to consider”). This file does not make that change.
  Question. Why might a later writer change “they” to “we,” and what is lost when that happens?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. “The crimson thread of kinship”
  This line is from the Melbourne banquet of 6 February 1890, not from Tenterfield. In the same
  speech Parkes spoke of a shared British origin. “Us all” was a claim about kinship. It was not a claim
  that every person on this continent was included. Aboriginal people, and many Chinese-Australians,
  were outside that “thread” as Parkes drew it.
  Question. If a speaker says “us all,” how can you tell who is meant?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. He never saw it happen
  Tenterfield, 24 October 1889. Melbourne banquet, 6 February 1890. Parkes died on 27 April 1896.
  The Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901. The handover line in this file is not a quotation from
  Parkes. It is this file’s plain statement of those dates.
  Question. Why might it matter that the man later called the “Father of Federation” — a later title, not
  a name he gave himself on the typographic page — never saw the ceremony?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  4. Who could vote in the referendums
  The Constitution was put to voters in 1898, 1899 and 1900. The rules were not the same in every
  colony. Women could vote in South Australia, and, from 1899, in Western Australia. In most other




                           Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   130

In some other colonies the picture is more complicated, and summaries sometimes flatten it. New South Wales’s 1898 result is often told as a majority that still failed
pages.text:
colonies the voters were adult men. Aboriginal people were widely excluded in Queensland and
Western Australia. In some other colonies the picture is more complicated, and summaries
sometimes flatten it. New South Wales’s 1898 result is often told as a majority that still failed a
special threshold; later votes went the other way. Western Australia voted in 1900. New Zealand did
not join.
Question. Why is “the people voted for Federation” too simple a sentence?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Section 127, and the race power
Section 127 of the Constitution, as it stood in 1901, said that in reckoning the numbers of the people,
“aboriginal natives shall not be counted.” Section 51(xxvi) gave the Commonwealth power to make
special laws for “the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State.” Both were
changed in 1967. This file does not treat those later changes as if they cancelled the 1901 record, or as
if they ended every question about who counts.
Question. What is the difference between not being counted, and not being allowed to vote?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. The 1902 Franchise Act, and section 41
The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902, assented to on 12 June, gave the federal vote to men and
women who met its tests — and then said: “No aboriginal native of Australia Asia Africa or the
Islands of the Pacific except New Zealand shall be entitled to have his name placed on an Electoral
Roll unless so entitled under section forty-one of the Constitution.” Section 41 is a difficult clause.
Later governments and courts often read it narrowly. This file flags that dispute rather than settling
it.
Question. Why might a law that is remembered for giving women the federal vote also be a record of
who was shut out?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Quong Tart’s letter, and the dictation test
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 used a dictation test to keep many people out. On 8 January
1903 Quong Tart wrote to Barton about how that law was affecting Chinese people. The National
Archives of Australia describes the letter; this file has not printed a word-for-word extract, because it
has not checked a full transcription against the original in this build. In 1894, Sir Henry Parkes had
written a letter of introduction for Quong Tart, praising his “energy and integrity.” Parkes’s “crimson
thread” and Parkes’s respect for one Chinese-Australian merchant can both be in the record.




                         Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   131

8. Barton’s line, and the day it was not said
“For the first time in history, we have a nation for a continent and a continent for a nation” is
recorded as Barton’s line at Ashfield in 1897. It is often later told as if it were said at Centennial Park
on 1 January 1901. This file keeps the 1897 date. A famous phrase can still be the wrong proof for a
day.
Question. Why might people want a great sentence to have been said on the nation’s first morning?

pages.text:
CASE 9 · YEAR 6 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
Draft, pending consultation. This case asks who was left out of the new nation, including
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Teach it with care. Follow AIATSIS guidance, and
do not treat this file as a finished account of First Nations experience. The user’s name is kept
off the student pages and off the app.


What is quoted, and what is framing
The typographic page is not a facsimile of a newspaper, and it is not a diary. It is a typographic
setting of verified wording. The Tenterfield lines are taken from The Sydney Morning Herald,
25 October 1889, p. 8, which reported the banquet speech of 24 October. The Herald used
reported speech. This file keeps “they had to consider,” “had done,” “could bring about,” and
“He believed that the time had come.” It does not rewrite those lines as “I” or “we.” Some later
museum and classroom pages do make that change. The Teacher Note flags them, rather than
following them.
The last line on the typographic page, “The crimson thread of kinship runs through us all,” is
from Parkes’s response to the toast “A United Australasia” at the Federation Conference
banquet in Queen’s Hall, Parliament House, Melbourne, on 6 February 1890. It is not from
Tenterfield. It is one of the most widely attested sentences in the Federation story. Teachers
should still check a contemporary report (The Argus or The Age, 7 February 1890, or a careful
later printing) beside this page.
“He never saw it happen” is this file’s handover. It is not a quotation from Parkes. The dates
under it are not in dispute: he died on 27 April 1896; the Commonwealth began on 1 January
1901. The file does not invent a Centennial Park scene in his voice, or a child’s invented diary of
that morning, on the student pages.


Care, and conflicts this file will not settle
Who could vote in each referendum is not a single rule. Women voted in South Australia, and in
Western Australia from 1899. Aboriginal voting was restricted or denied in Queensland and
Western Australia; elsewhere the picture is more complicated, and secondary summaries
sometimes flatten it. Section 41 of the Constitution, and how it was later applied to people
already on a state roll, is still argued over. The 1902 Act’s exclusion is quoted from the Act itself
(assented 12 June 1902). “Father of Federation” is a later title. Barton’s “nation for a continent”
line is kept at Ashfield, 1897, not moved to 1 January 1901. This file summarises Quong Tart’s 8
January 1903 letter from the National Archives’ description; it does not print a word-for-word
extract, because a full checked transcription of that letter was not in hand for this build.
Parkes’s 1 March 1894 letter of introduction for Quong Tart is in the State Library of New South
Wales papers.
Rose Scott’s card does not invent a quotation. A later parliamentary-library account has been
cited elsewhere for words of hers about race, colour, and the 1902 franchise. Those words were

Resources
Students can also read Parkes’s typographic page as an interactive book, on a tablet or
phone. The page on screen is the same story as the pages in this book. Use it in class, or
send the link home. The app is built and ready; it should be published only when you say
go. The QR code uses a seven-pointed Federation star at the centre.

Australian Constitution as enacted, sections 51(xxvi), 41 and 127; Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902,
especially sections 3 and 4; Immigration Restriction Act 1901; National Archives of Australia, letter from

A notebook, opened more than a century later
                                                    New Year’s Day, 1915 — and now
They packed for a picnic.
That’s the bit I can’t get past. Ore wagons with benches in them.
Sandwiches. About a thousand people going to Silverton, and a
girl my age on the train, sitting next to someone she liked.
They saw an ice-cream cart by the line, and a flag, and two men.
Some of them thought the shots were for the new year. Then the
shots weren’t.
Four people were killed. Seven were hurt. That night a crowd
burned the German Club, and the police had to stand in front of a
mosque so the same crowd wouldn’t go there next.

 I keep looking for a clean reason. The notes they left
don’t give me one I can live with. Neither does what the
                     town did after.

CASE 10 · YEAR 9 · THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · READ
The Battle of Broken Hill, 1 January 1915
Why did they do it, and was the backlash fair?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  On the morning of 1 January 1915, a picnic train left Broken Hill for Silverton for the annual
  Manchester Unity Oddfellows picnic. The Barrier Miner, printed the same day, said the train left
  Sulphide-street station at 10 a.m., and that it consisted of two brake vans and 40 ore trucks,
  “with a freight of some 1200 picnickers on board.” Some later accounts say 41 carriages. This file
  records both, and does not choose.




  Beside the line, an ice-cream cart was flying a small red flag with a white crescent and star — the
  Ottoman (Turkish) flag. Two men, later named as Gool Badsha Mahomed (the spelling of his
  name varies) and Mullah Abdullah, fired on the train. Four people were killed: Alma Priscilla
  Cowie, aged 17, a passenger; William John Shaw, aged 46, a passenger; Alfred Millard, who was
  riding a bicycle beside the line (his middle name is given as Elton in the NSW Police Gazette and
  some official reports, and as Elvin in some later accounts); and James Craig, aged 69, who was
  in his yard and was hit during the later gunfight, not on the train. Seven other people were
  wounded, including Constable Robert Mills.




  Police, military men under Lieutenant Resch, and armed civilians pursued the two men to a
  quartz outcrop later known as White Rocks. Both men were shot. Abdullah was found dead.
  Gool was badly wounded and died in hospital. Sources disagree on how long the gunfight lasted:
  about 40 minutes in one later museum account; almost two hours in others.




  Notes were found. Contemporary reports and later summaries do not all give the same wording.
  They agree that the notes linked the attack to the Ottoman Sultan and to the writers’ faith, and

that Abdullah’s note also named a grudge against Chief Sanitary Inspector Cornelius Brosnan,
who had prosecuted him for slaughtering animals away from the licensed abattoir. Gool’s note is
widely reported to have been written for him by Abdullah, because Gool was illiterate. This file
has not inspected the original notes.




That night a crowd in Broken Hill attacked and set fire to the German Club. Police later
described the building as “maliciously set fire to and destroyed.” The club’s trustees offered a
reward of £25; the state government matched it. Police and military were also sent to the North
Camel Camp and the mosque, after a crowd moved in that direction. Officers later returned to
the mosque because they had entered it without removing their boots.




Local Muslim residents were threatened. The two men’s bodies were buried by police at an
undisclosed place. A coronial inquest on the four victims opened, was adjourned, and was held
on 7 January 1915; an inquiry into the deaths of Gool and Abdullah followed the next day. The
coroner found that the four had died from gunshot wounds feloniously inflicted by the two men,
and that the shooting of the two men was justifiable.




Gool and Abdullah were Muslim men who had lived at the cameleers’ camp. Police records and
newspapers did not agree on their nationality, and often called them Turks because of the flag.
Later accounts describe Abdullah as probably from Afghanistan or a neighbouring region,
literate in Dari, and Gool as an Afridi man from the Tirah region who had earlier served in the
Ottoman army and, by 1915, sold ice-cream in Broken Hill. The Ottoman Empire had entered
the war against Britain in late October 1914.

My finding
CASE 10 · YEAR 9 · THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are M. Kenny, the notes the two men left, and the police record of that night. Further
people — including Walhanna Asson, Cornelius Brosnan, and the local Muslim community — are in Super Sleuths.

You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is
not a 1915 diary. Say what you think the records can prove about why the two men fired, and
whether the town’s answer that night was fair. “We can’t know” is an honest finding when the
notes conflict, or when the record of the riot is thinner than the record of the shooting. Do not
invent what the sources do not say. Treat the dead, and the living families of this story, with
care.

Why did they do it, and was the backlash fair?
Circle one: They did it as an act of war for the Ottoman Sultan · They did it because of a local grudge
and years of being shut out · Both of those things were tangled together, and we can’t separate them
cleanly · The backlash was not fair, even if the shooting was a crime · We can’t know, from this
file, all of why they did it, or how far the town’s anger spread · Another finding, written below

Why it still matters
The “Battle of Broken Hill” is still told as a curiosity of the First World War on Australian soil,
and sometimes as if it were simple. The file is open because the notes do not all say the same
thing, because a picnic train is not a battlefield, and because the night that followed — a burned
club, a guarded mosque, a secret burial — is part of the same case. How a town answers a crime,
and who it answers it upon, still matters.

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. James Craig was not on the train
Three people were killed in the attack on the train and the pipe track: Alma Cowie, William Shaw,
and Alfred Millard. James Craig was in his yard, about a hundred yards from the Cable Hotel, and
was hit during the later gunfight. A stepdaughter urged him to come inside. Treating all four deaths
as if they happened in the ore wagons flattens the day.
Question. Why does it matter, for a finding, where each of the four was when they were hit?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Walhanna Asson, and the camel camp
Walhanna Asson, a Punjabi-speaking camel-owner from Peshawar, carried water to a wounded
constable while under fire, and was himself nearly shot by late-comers who took him for “one of the
enemy” until police protected him. That night a crowd moved on the mosque. Officers later went back
because they had entered it in boots. Local Muslims protested when a gravedigger began two graves
in their cemetery for the two attackers. The backlash did not fall only on a club that happened to be
German.
Question. If you are asked whether the backlash was fair, whose evidence belongs in the answer —
the burned club, the guarded mosque, Asson, or all of them?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. Were “all Germans” already interned?
Some later retellings say the German Club stood empty because every German in Australia had
already been interned. That is too strong for 1 January 1915. Internment of “enemy aliens” happened
during the war, and it was not a single clean sweep on one day. The club was burned. German
residents were threatened. How many people were in the club that night, and how internment later
widened, should be checked, not assumed.
Question. What happens to a story about backlash if you write, wrongly, that the target building was
already empty of the people it stood for?

Teacher Note
CASE 10 · YEAR 9 · THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · TEACHER NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page. The user’s name is kept off the student pages and off
the app.


What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed Year 10 student notebook, written for this file, in an
angsty voice. It is not a 1915 diary and not the voice of a named historical person. “A girl my
age” is Alma Priscilla Cowie, 17; the opener does not invent her thoughts or last words. Violence
is named, not described in graphic detail. No death photographs are used anywhere in the file.


Curriculum
The brief asked for an accurate AC9HS9 code. There is no AC9HS9. Year 9 History uses
AC9HH9 codes. The lead code is AC9HH9K11: the effects of the First World War on Australian
society. The shooting happened on Australian soil in January 1915, after the Ottoman Empire
had entered the war; the aftermath includes a riot, a burned German Club, and the treatment of
a local Muslim community. AC9HH9K09 (places Australians fought) is not used as the lead,
because this was not a campaign overseas.


Source conflicts, flagged
Alma / Elma Cowie; Alfred Elton / Elvin Millard; 40 trucks / 41 carriages; “some 1200”
picnickers; gunfight of about 40 minutes / almost two hours; varied spellings of Gool Badsha
Mahomed (Gool, Goul, Mahomed, Mohammed, Mahommed). Translations of the notes do not
all match. Later “planted flag” / forged letter claims are not treated as agreed. Overstatements
that “every German” had already been interned are flagged. Shaw worked in the sanitary
department; the man named in Abdullah’s note is Inspector Brosnan, not Shaw.


Religion, race, and care
Gool and Abdullah were Muslim. The local cameleer community was not the same as the two
men. Teach the faith, and the camp, with respect. Do not let the word “Turk,” which 1915 papers
used because of the flag, erase that uncertainty. Living families, including descendants of
victims and of the camel camp, deserve legal and ethical care even though the principals are
long dead. Year 9–10 students can hold two things at once: the killing of civilians was a crime,
and a riot against other people’s club, camp and mosque still has to be judged.


Country
Broken Hill is on Wilyakali Country. This file does not tell a First Nations history of the event,
and does not invent one. A deeper local treatment would need consultation. The student pages
do not pretend otherwise.

20 February 1965
                                                                                            Moree

Egg on my sleeve. I keep wiping it. Still there.

We came back. We had to. Last time they said the ban was off. We left. They put it
back on. I don’t know why I thought a meeting would be enough.

The crowd was already at the pool. Pressing in. So hot I could hardly breathe.
Someone spat. Then the tomatoes, the eggs. I have never been looked at like that.

I keep thinking we don’t live here. We’re from Sydney. We get on the bus. The
children don’t.

The police said if we stayed it would get worse. We stayed. I wanted to go. I hate
that I wanted to go.

Charlie wouldn’t move from the gate. They grabbed him. For a moment I couldn’t see
the kids and I thought —

I thought I would be braver than this.

One of the children was knocked down. They were frightened. So was I. What a thing
to come all this way and still be frightened.

They let them in, in the end. We went in too. For a minute it felt like winning. Then
we had to walk to the bus in a single line and they were still throwing things and
the windows kept getting hit.

A man at the bus said it quietly.

They’ll wait till you’re gone.

                                                                                     — on the bus

The Freedom Ride · New South Wales, February 1965
Draft, pending consultation with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially Moree and

Read the notebook page through to the last line. Then read what the 1965 file can agree on. After
that, three people will be asked the same three questions.

  CASE FILE: FREEDOM RIDE / 1965
  Date of incident      12–26 February 1965 (Moree visits: 16 and 19–20 February)
  Location          Regional New South Wales, including Walgett and Moree
  Status             Unresolved contradictions · Draft, pending consultation
  Key claims still disputed
  – What actually changed in the towns, and for how long?
  – Whose record should we trust — student diaries, local Aboriginal accounts, or the 1965
  newspapers and television?
  – When was the Moree baths ban really lifted?




  WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1965 FILE, AND AFTER
  Twenty-nine University of Sydney students left around midnight on 12 February 1965, as Student Action
  for Aborigines (SAFA). Charles Perkins, an Arrernte man, was president. Some left later and others joined.

  They travelled through regional New South Wales for about two weeks, using surveys, pickets and
  cameras, and they kept diaries. Newspapers, radio and television reported the trip as it happened.

  They went to Moree twice. On 16 February, Aboriginal children were at first refused the baths, then let in.
  That evening a public meeting voted 88 to 10 to remove the segregation clause.

  After they left, the old 1955 rule was enforced again. They returned on 19–20 February. A hostile crowd
  met them at the pool. Eggs, tomatoes and stones were thrown. Children and students went in, then left
  that night through the crowd.

  Local Aboriginal people were already campaigning in towns such as Walgett. The students met Harry Hall,
  president of the Walgett Aborigines’ Progressive Association, on 15 February.

  The Moree baths rule used the period language of racial exclusion. The wording is in Super Sleuths, with a
  content note. The ban was not settled in a single day.

CASE 12 · YEAR 10 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher note
Draft, pending consultation with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially
Moree and Walgett, and those they name, and with AIATSIS guidance.


The opener
The notebook is constructed. It is not an original 1965 page, and the handwriting is not original.
That fact belongs only in this teacher note, not on the student page. The writer is an unnamed city
student on the bus, in the spirit of diaries kept on the trip; the page is not Ann Curthoys’s diary and
must not be taught as hers. The date is 20 February 1965, the second Moree visit, after the first
meeting and after the ban was put back on. Scene details — the reimposed ban, the hostile crowd,
spit, eggs, tomatoes, stones, the police warning, Perkins taken from the gate, a child knocked down,
frightened children, going in, and leaving in single file while things were still being thrown — follow
Ann Curthoys’s contemporary diary (AIATSIS collection; published 2002) and Charles Perkins’s
later account of the return, as quoted on the AIATSIS Freedom Ride page. The draft’s “four nights
ago,” the 16 February date, the SAFA title, the method-explaining paragraph, the 88-to-10 vote, the
by-law wording, the number aboard, Gary Williams, and Lismore were taken off this page. They
belong in What is agreed, Super Sleuths, or this note.

Two short conversations in the source draft — a twelve-year-old who had never been inside, and a
woman from the mission — were invented details inside a known sequence. They have been cut.
Two scene lines were checked against the 20 February record and kept. “Charlie wouldn’t move
from the gate. They grabbed him.” Curthoys’s diary of the return, as quoted by AIATSIS, records:
“Charlie started talking to the crowd, but there was a lot of hissing and booing. Then he went to the
front of the line and when he refused to move was grabbed and taken away from the line.” Perkins,
in A Bastard Like Me (1975), also quoted by AIATSIS, places the struggle at the gate: “The mayor
ordered the police to have us removed from the gate entrance. They took hold of my arm and the
struggle started.” The notebook’s “from the gate” is a short compression of those two accounts of the
same confrontation. “One of the children was knocked down.” Curthoys’s diary, as quoted by
AIATSIS, records: “One child had been knocked down. The poor kids were very frightened.” She
wrote that the children told the students this, and that they had also been subjected to racist abuse
(the wording is not repeated on the student pages). Contemporary newspaper headlines of 21–22
February 1965 report a violent confrontation at Moree (among them the Daily Mirror, 21 February,
and the Sydney Morning Herald, 22 February). This file did not independently recover those two
exact phrases from a Trove article body. The closing is now: “A man at the bus said it quietly.” then
“They’ll wait till you’re gone.” Both the speaker and the line are constructed. The man is not a
named historical person. Do not teach either as a documented 1965 quotation. The line stands in for
a documented pattern: after the first Moree visit the ban was reimposed once the bus had left, and
later Moree memory records a similar fear. In 2025, Gomeroi man Uncle Darryl French, who was on
the bus to the pool on the return visit, recalled people saying that when the students left, local
people would have to deal with it (ABC News, 22 February 2025). Living people, including French,
are not given dates on the student pages.

Corrections and flags
Two Moree visits, not one. The source draft merged them. First visit, Wednesday 16 February
1965: a picket; children at first refused, then let in; an evening public meeting at the Memorial Hall,
initially hostile, at which a motion to remove the segregation clause was carried 88 votes to 10
(Curthoys’s diary, via AIATSIS; also ABC News, 2025). On 17 February, after the students had left,
Aboriginal children tried to get in after school; the mayor then said the 6 June 1955 statute would be
enforced (Curthoys, 18 February entry). In Tenterfield the students voted to return. Second visit,
Saturday 19–Sunday 20 February: a hostile crowd; eggs, tomatoes, stones, spit and scuffles; the
mayor said he would sign a motion to rescind, with conditions; children and students went in; they
left that night in single file (Curthoys’s diary; Perkins, A Bastard Like Me, via AIATSIS; ABC News,
2019 and 2025). Do not teach the ban as settled on 16 February. Curthoys later recalled that it took
about six months before the council formally rescinded the rule (ABC News, 27 September 2019).

Route and Lismore. The students left Sydney around midnight on Friday 12 February. A day-by-
day itinerary published by AIATSIS is: 12 Sydney; 13 Wellington; 14 Gulargambone; 15 Walgett; 16
Moree (first); 17 Boggabilla; 18 Tenterfield, then back; 19–20 Moree (return); 21 Grafton; 22
Lismore and Cabbage Tree Island; 23 Bowraville; 24 Kempsey; 25 Taree; 26 Sydney. They did not
leave for Lismore after the first Moree meeting. Some other lists add towns such as Warwick, Glen
Innes, Inverell or Coffs Harbour; treat those as a minor conflict in the route lists, not a problem to
resolve on the student page.

Numbers aboard. Twenty-nine students left Sydney on 12 February (University of Sydney;
Sydney Barani; AIATSIS). About 35 took part in all, because some left and others joined (AIATSIS).
Keep 29 as the departure figure, and flag that the complement changed.

By-law wording. The draft shortened the rule to “No person being a full-blooded or half-caste
aboriginal… shall use the baths.” ABC News (22 February 2025) quotes a fuller wording, used in
Super Sleuths with a content note. Wording and spelling vary slightly across later accounts; this file
has not checked the 1955 council instrument itself. The statute is often dated 6 June 1955
(Curthoys).

Gary Williams. A Gumbaynggirr-Bundjalung student, and one of two Aboriginal students at the
University of Sydney with Perkins. He was a member of SAFA, but he was not on the bus from
Sydney and he was not at either Moree visit. He was called home for a family emergency and joined
at Bowraville on 23 February, later confining his activism to locations on his own country
(University of Sydney, 2024; NSWALC; Sydney Barani; ABC News, 2025). The draft’s line that he
was “meant to join us later” and would “only come on the stretch that is his own country” over-
explains the delay. He is living: no dates on the student pages. He is named only in Super Sleuths
and this note.

Perkins’s words and graduation. “The problem is out in the open now” is kept, cited from
AIATSIS as said at the 1965 FCAATSI conference in Canberra, to about 200 people. This file has not
independently checked a 1965 conference transcript. The phrase “second class is not good enough”
appears in later interviews and education pages; it has not been pinned here to a 1965 primary
source, and it is not used on the student pages. Do not call Perkins “the first Aboriginal person to
graduate.” He graduated from the University of Sydney in 1966, and is often described as the first
Aboriginal man to do so; Margaret Valadian graduated from the University of Queensland in the



                          Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   158

pages.text:
same year, and is acknowledged as the first Aboriginal woman to complete an Australian university
degree. Valadian is living: no dates on the student pages. The graduation claim is omitted from the
student card.

A misattributed quotation. The source draft gave Ann Curthoys the line that the ride “convinced
a very wide section of the public that things were very, very bad.” That wording is Jim Spigelman’s,
in a BBC interview published in 2015, not Curthoys’s. It has been removed from her card.

The third witness. The source draft used a group card, “Local Aboriginal voices.” This file names
Harry Hall, president of the Walgett Aborigines’ Progressive Association in 1965, because a
documented local Aboriginal person from that year, with a citable role, is a better fit for the three-
witness pattern. He met the students in Walgett; local campaigning was already underway, with
others including Ted Fields; later in 1965 he asked Perkins to return over the colour bar at the Oasis
Hotel (AIATSIS; ABC News, 2025; Walgett AMS Freedom Ride project). The card is lean on
purpose: it is not a 1965 first-person diary, and later family memory (including Amy Townsend’s
account of her grandfather) belongs in discussion, not as if it were written in February 1965. Do not
conflate him with his son, Harry Phillip Hall, who is living, who also assisted in 1965, and who must
not be given dates on a student page. Other later Moree and Bowraville oral histories — including
Wayne Nean and Aunty Sandra Buchanan, both living — are options for a future revision after
consultation, not extra cards in this draft.


Pictures, language, and care
The three images are plain mid-century-style silhouettes with name cards, not likenesses of the
people named. No portrait has been invented. A 1965 photograph of Perkins, from the State Library
of New South Wales Tribune set, appears on Wikimedia Commons as Flickr Commons “no known
copyright restrictions,” but the library catalogue also records courtesy of Tribune / SEARCH
Foundation. This draft uses a silhouette until rights and consultation are settled. Student pages
avoid slur-spelled-out language and keep violence at the level the diaries record (eggs, tomatoes,
stones, spit, shoving, a child knocked down). Teacher preview is required. Period wording appears
only as a short attributed extract, with a content note.


Consultation and teaching
Consultation first, with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited in 1965 — especially Moree
(Gamilaraay / Gomeroi) and Walgett (Wayilwan, Gamilaraay and Yuwaalaraay), and the other
communities on the route — and with those they name, following AIATSIS guidance. Use the
community’s own names for Country. Local protest did not begin when the bus arrived. Do not let a
Sydney student notebook stand in for a local Aboriginal account. AIATSIS Code of Ethics; guidelines
for ethical publishing; free, prior and informed consent; agreement on what may be quoted. No
sacred or secret material. This case is a draft, not a finished student file.

significant individuals and groups in the campaign for the recognition of the rights of First Nations
Australians, and the extent to which they brought change. AC9HH10K11, significant events and

CASE 13 · YEAR 10 · READ
What can the records prove?
The Perth Mint Swindle, 1982
This file names living people. It does not say that any living person committed the swindle, or
fabricated evidence. Attribute every claim. The 2004 court quashed the convictions. It did not decide
who obtained the gold. No one has been convicted of the swindle since.
Read the 1989 page through to the last line. Then read what this file can agree on. After that, three
witnesses will be asked the same three questions.

  CASE FILE: PERTH MINT SWINDLE / 1982
  Date of incident      22 June 1982 (gold returned, in part, 1989; convictions quashed 2 July
  2004)
  Location          Perth, Western Australia
  Status    Convictions quashed · Who obtained the gold remains
  undecided
  Key claims still disputed
  – What can the 1982–2004 records actually prove?
  – How far can Lewandowski’s 2002 affidavit be trusted?
  – The court quashed the convictions. Did it decide who obtained the gold?




  WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1982–2008 FILE
  On 22 June 1982, gold left the Perth Mint in exchange for three stolen building-society cheques. The
  quantity is usually given as 49 bars, about 68 kilograms, then valued at about $653,000. Couriers collected
  it. The investigation said it was taken to an office in Subiaco and later towards Jandakot Airport. It then
  disappeared.

  Ray, Peter and Brian Mickelberg were charged and, in 1983, convicted in the District Court of Western
  Australia (Heenan CJDC). Ray was sentenced to 20 years, Peter to 16 years, and Brian to 12 years. Brian’s
  convictions were quashed on appeal in November 1983, and he was released after about nine months. He
  died in a plane crash in 1986.

  In 1989, gold later identified with the missing bullion was sent, anonymously, to Channel 7 in Perth. First,
  a bar was sent to the reporter Alison Fan, with a note. About three months later, gold pellets in containers
  were left at the station. The Mint said the gold matched what had left in 1982. The convictions of Ray and
  Peter still stood.

  In June 2002, former detective Tony Lewandowski swore an affidavit about the investigation. He said that
  he and Don Hancock had fabricated the notes of interview dated 26 July 1982, after 2 September 1982,
  and that evidence they had given about those “confessions” was false. Hancock had died in 2001.
  Lewandowski died in 2004. Hancock was never charged or convicted of fabricating evidence.

  On 2 July 2004 the Court of Criminal Appeal of Western Australia, in Mickelberg v The Queen [2004]
  WASCA 145, allowed the appeals of Ray and Peter, quashed their convictions, and did not order a retrial.

The majority was Malcolm CJ and Steytler J. Murray J dissented. The court found a substantial
  miscarriage of justice. It did not decide who obtained the gold. No one has been convicted of the swindle

  In December 2007, the WA Police Commissioner, Karl O’Callaghan, issued a public apology, in the context
  of a defamation settlement over comments made after the 2004 judgment. The statement said the police
  accepted the court’s decision, and that Ray and Peter were, and remained, entitled to the presumption of
  innocence. In January 2008 the State Government announced an ex gratia payment of $500,000 to each
  of them, in addition to money already paid toward legal costs of the later appeals. A 2021 ex gratia
  payment has not been found in the sources checked for this file.

Ray and Peter Mickelberg
                                The two brothers whose 1983 convictions were quashed in 2004 · Living — no dates

                                Their own accounts, from arrest through the appeals and after the convictions were

                                Source. Public statements and evidence over many years, including accounts considered in Mickelberg v
                                The Queen [2004] WASCA 145. Living people: no dates, and no photographs, on these pages.
                                What they said. They have always said they did not take the gold. They say police,
A silhouette, not a likeness.   including Don Hancock and Tony Lewandowski, fabricated admissions. Peter has said that,
                                after his arrest on 26 July 1982, he was stripped and assaulted at Belmont. They have also
                                said that a fingerprint used in the case was not honestly obtained. That last claim is their
                                allegation. This file does not treat it as a court finding.
                                Could they really have seen it? They were there for their own arrests, interviews and trials.
                                They could not see everything the police did with documents when they were not in the room.

                                part of what Peter had said about the interview and the notes. The 2004 court did not decide
                                who obtained the gold.
                                Why might they say it? To have the convictions set aside, and to be believed. An account
                                maintained for many years is still one side of a contested file. It has to be weighed with the
                                court’s reasons, not instead of them.

The three witness cards on the last pages are Ray and Peter Mickelberg, Tony Lewandowski, and the Court of
Criminal Appeal. Further people and claims — including Brian Mickelberg, Alison Fan, Don Hancock, and later
allegations about a fingerprint — are in Super Sleuths. This finding is about what the records can prove, not about

You have a 1989 page, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is one reported
sentence from 1989, set in type. It is not the whole record. Say what you think the records can
prove, what the court actually decided, and what you still can’t know. Do not name a living

Why it still matters
The Perth Mint swindle is still told as a thriller, and as a scandal about the police and the
courts. The file is open because the 2004 court quashed the convictions and did not decide who
obtained the gold, and because no one has been convicted of the swindle since. What a court
decides, and what a story claims, are not the same thing.

  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The two deliveries in 1989
  Gold later identified with the missing bullion reached Channel 7 in Perth twice in 1989. First, in July,
  a bar was sent to the reporter Alison Fan, with a note. About three months later, gold pellets in
  containers were left at the station after a journalist was tipped off. The Mint said the gold matched
  what had left in 1982.
  The wording of the July note is later reported by ABC News (1 April 2023) as: “The Mickelbergs are
  innocent and rotting in jail.” A contemporaneous 1989 clipping with that exact sentence was not
  located for this file. A second note was reported with the later pellets; its exact wording is not
  securely established here. The opening page uses only the later-reported July sentence, set in type. It
  is not a photograph of the original note.
  Question. What can a returned bar, and a short unsigned sentence, actually prove — and what can
  they not?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. What the 2004 court decided — and what it did not
  Read Mickelberg v The Queen [2004] WASCA 145 (2 July 2004) on AustLII, at least the orders and
  the majority’s conclusions. The petitioners were Raymond John Mickelberg and Peter Mickelberg.
  Brian was not a petitioner in 2004.
  The majority (Malcolm CJ and Steytler J) allowed the appeals, quashed the convictions, and did not
  order a retrial. They found a substantial miscarriage of justice, and a significant possibility that a
  reasonable jury would have acquitted in the light of the fresh evidence. They held that the remaining
  circumstantial evidence did not make guilt inevitable — including that Peter had not been positively
  identified at the vehicle on 22 June 1982. Murray J dissented. The court did not decide who obtained
  the gold.
  Question. In your own words, separate the court’s orders from the stories people still tell about the
  case.




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. A recanting police witness
  In June 2002, after Don Hancock’s death, Tony Lewandowski swore an affidavit. As later reported

4. The fingerprint — an allegation, not a finding in this file
It has been alleged that a fingerprint used in the case was not honestly obtained. Some later news
features have stated that claim as fact. This file does not. The 2004 court is the place to look for what
was actually found, and what was left as dispute. Keep this claim out of “What is agreed.”
Question. How would you mark a serious allegation on a case file, so that a later reader does not
mistake it for a court finding?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. The apology, and the payment — 2007 and 2008, not 2021
On 15 December 2007, Commissioner Karl O’Callaghan issued a public apology on behalf of WA
Police, in the context of a defamation settlement after comments made on the day of the 2004
judgment. The statement said the police accepted the court’s decision, and that Ray and Peter were,
and remained, entitled to the presumption of innocence.
On 16 January 2008 the State Government announced an ex gratia payment of $500,000 to each of
them, in addition to $658,672 already paid toward legal representation in later appeals. The brothers
described the offer as “take it or leave it,” and said it was too low; they remained free to pursue civil
claims against individuals. A 2021 ex gratia payment has not been found in the sources checked for
this file.
Question. What is the difference between a court quashing a conviction, a police apology, and an ex
gratia payment?

Teacher Note
CASE 13 · YEAR 10 · TEACHER NOTE


This file names living people. It does not say that any living person committed the swindle, or
fabricated evidence. Attribute every claim. The 2004 court quashed the convictions. It did not
decide who obtained the gold. No one has been convicted of the swindle since.


Where this case sits, and why
The user’s draft numbered this Case 39, Year 10, and gave the codes AC9HH10K10 and
AC9HH10K11. In the year-level list, Case 39 is already Zelda D’Aprano and equal pay, 1969. This file
does not overwrite that case. It is placed as Case 13, Year 10, the next free number. Year 10 is the
right band (a late-twentieth-century Australian debate that runs into the 2000s).

AC9HH10K10 and AC9HH10K11 are Year 10 knowledge descriptions about First Nations rights and
freedoms. They are the wrong codes for this file. The honest History knowledge code used here is
AC9HH10K20: different historical interpretations and debates during the second half of the
twentieth century. A related Civics description, AC9HC10K03 (the role of courts and how rights are
protected), may be mentioned to teachers; it is not claimed as a History code on the student pages.


The opening page
The 1989 page is a typographic setting, not a photograph of the original note, and not a facsimile.
That explanation is kept off the student page so the opener can be read as a scene. The only sentence
set as the note is the wording later reported by ABC News, 1 April 2023: “The Mickelbergs are
innocent and rotting in jail.” A contemporaneous 1989 clipping with that exact sentence was not
located for this file. If a teacher has a 1989 source with different wording, the typographic page
should be revised to match the better source, and this note should say so.

There were two deliveries in 1989, not one. In July, a bar was sent to Channel 7 reporter Alison Fan,
with a note. About three months later, pellets in containers were left at the station. A second note
was reported; its exact wording is not securely established here, so it is not quoted as if it were. The
draft’s constructed four-line note (“The Mickelbergs are innocent. / This is from the Mint. / The rest
is still out there. / The police lied.”) was not used, and must not be presented as a real document.
Alison Fan is living: she may be named, but is not given dates, and is not photographed.


Legal care
Do not state or imply, in the book’s voice, that any living person committed the swindle, or that any
living person fabricated evidence, unless a court has found it. Attribute every claim. The 2004 court
(Mickelberg v The Queen [2004] WASCA 145, 2 July 2004) allowed the appeals of Ray and Peter,
quashed their convictions, and ordered no retrial. The majority was Malcolm CJ and Steytler J;
Murray J dissented. The majority found a substantial miscarriage of justice, and a significant
possibility that a reasonable jury would have acquitted in the light of the fresh evidence. It did not
decide who obtained the gold. No one has been convicted of the swindle since. Living people



                          Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample ·   172

pages.alt: Page 173. Case 13. (including Ray and Peter Mickelberg, and others still living) get no dates and no photographs. Silhouettes are used, and are labelled as silhouettes, not likenesses. Silhouettes are used, and are labelled as silhouettes, not likenesses. The court card is a scales
symbol, not a judge’s portrait.

Tony Lewandowski’s 2002 affidavit is a source the 2004 court considered. It is his sworn claim,
reported at the time (including the Sydney Morning Herald, 11 June 2002) and weighed in the
judgment. He admitted that evidence he had given earlier was false. He died in 2004, before the
July judgment. Do not put graphic detail of his death on student pages. Don Hancock (died 2001)
was never charged or convicted of fabricating evidence. Claims about him should remain attributed
(for example, “Lewandowski swore that…”). Hancock’s later public controversies (including Ora
Banda and other unproven matters) are kept off the student pages. They are not proof of what
happened in the 1982–83 Mint investigation.

It has been alleged that a fingerprint was planted or was not honestly obtained. Some later features,
including ABC News on 1 April 2023, have stated that as fact. This file does not. The claim is kept
out of “What is agreed,” and appears in Super Sleuths only as an allegation. The same 2023 feature
places the trial in the Supreme Court; the 2004 judgment records it as a District Court trial before
Heenan CJDC (IND 675 of 1982). Prefer the judgment.

The brief’s reference to a 2021 ex gratia payment and apology was checked and not found. The
documented dates are 15 December 2007 (WA Police apology, Commissioner Karl O’Callaghan, in
the context of a defamation settlement after comments by Assistant Commissioner Mel Hay on 2
July 2004) and 16 January 2008 (State Government ex gratia payment of $500,000 to each of Ray
and Peter, announced by Attorney-General Jim McGinty, in addition to $658,672 already paid
toward legal costs of the 1998 and 2004 appeals). ABC reporting at the time put the combined figure
at more than $1.6 million. The brothers said the offer was “take it or leave it” and too low; they
remained free to pursue civil claims against individuals. The police statement accepted the court’s
decision and acknowledged that Ray and Peter were, and remained, entitled to the presumption of
innocence.

Brian Mickelberg: several reports say his appeal was allowed and his convictions quashed on 4
November 1983, and that he was released after about eight or nine months. ABC News, 1 April 2023,
says his sentence was “cut to eight months.” Those accounts conflict. The student page uses a careful
wording: released after about nine months following an appeal in 1983–84; died in a plane crash in
1986. Do not treat the ABC wording as settled. Sentences at trial are given here as Ray 20 years,
Peter 16 years, Brian 12 years (ABC 2023; the user’s draft; other summaries). One Sydney Morning
Herald piece has referred to a 14-year term for Peter; 16 is the better-attested figure. Ray served a
little over eight years; Peter more than six and a half.

An Australian Financial Review report of the later 1989 pellets described “one of 22 gold bars.” The
usual figure for the 1982 theft is 49 bars, about 68 kilograms, valued at about $653,000 (sometimes
given more exactly as $652,975.24). This file does not adopt “22 bars” on the student pages.


Curriculum and classroom
Year 10. The useful work is to separate a court’s orders from a story, to attribute a recanting witness,
and to sit with an unsolved question without inventing a culprit. The finding options deliberately
include “the records do not prove who obtained the gold” and “we can’t know.” Do not accept a

History. Last period.
                                                                   The photocopy is dated 3 June 1992

They keep saying terra nullius like it’s a spell they already broke.

I wrote it in my book and then I looked at the date. 3 June 1992. He was already
dead.

The first sheet is a man on Mer saying his father told him the land would be his.
The next sheet is a Queensland Act. The islands, it says, were “freed from all other
rights, interests and claims of any kind whatsoever.” No compensation was or is
payable.

I don’t know how a place with people on it gets called nobody’s land. I don’t even
know if they used those Latin words at the time. Miss said historians still argue
about the phrase. She didn’t say it like it was a relief.

I keep turning back to the bit where he talks about generations on the same
ground. It isn’t loud. That’s what I can’t get out of my head.

                             He never heard the judgment.

— in the margin

CASE 14 · YEAR 10 · MABO AND TERRA NULLIUS, 1982–1992 · READ
Mabo and terra nullius, 1982–1992
Was Australia ever really treated as ‘nobody’s land’?


What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.


  Eddie Koiki Mabo was a Meriam man from Mer (Murray Island) in the Torres Strait. In May
  1982 he and other Meriam plaintiffs, including David Passi, Sam Passi, Celuia Mapo Salee and
  James Rice, began a case in the High Court about ownership of land on the Murray Islands.




  While the case was running, the Queensland Parliament passed the Queensland Coast Islands
  Declaratory Act 1985. Section 3 declared that, on annexation, the islands “were vested in the
  Crown in right of Queensland freed from all other rights, interests and claims of any kind
  whatsoever.” Section 5 said no compensation “was or is payable.”




  In Mabo v Queensland (No 1), decided 8 December 1988, the High Court held that the 1985 Act
  was invalid to the extent it was inconsistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth). The
  land case could go on.




  Eddie Mabo died on 21 January 1992. On 3 June 1992, in Mabo v Queensland (No 2), six of the
  seven High Court justices held that the common law of Australia can recognise native title, and
  that the Meriam people were entitled, as against the whole world, to the possession, use,
  occupation and enjoyment of most of the lands of the Murray Islands (subject to some particular
  Crown interests).




  Justice Brennan’s leading reasons discussed and rejected what he called an “enlarged notion of

                                 A written judgment, not a speech from the street.
                                 What they said
                                 Brennan J wrote that “the fiction by which the rights and interests of
                                 indigenous inhabitants in land were treated as non-existent was justified by
                                 a policy which has no place in the contemporary law of this country.” He
A silhouette, not a likeness.
                                 also wrote: “It is imperative in today’s world that the common law should
 Official judicial portraits
   remain in copyright.          neither be nor be seen to be frozen in an age of racial discrimination.” He
                                 said the common law “would perpetuate injustice if it were to continue to
                                 embrace the enlarged notion of terra nullius and persist in characterizing
                                 the indigenous inhabitants of the Australian colonies as people too low in
                                 the scale of social organization to be acknowledged as possessing rights and
                                 interests in land.”
                                 Could they have seen it?
                                 He was deciding a case in 1992, from evidence and earlier law, including
                                 findings made in the Queensland Supreme Court. He was not an eyewitness
                                 to 1788, or to life on Mer. A judgment is an official interpretation of the law,
                                 written for a reason, by a judge in the majority.
                                 Why might they say it?
                                 To explain why the Court would no longer treat Indigenous people as if they
                                 had no rights in land, and to give reasons for recognising native title in
                                 Australian common law.
                                 Source. Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23; (1992) 175 CLR 1, Brennan J. The
                                 judgment is on AustLII.

The State of Queensland
                                  Defendant in the Mabo litigation · Parliament of Queensland, 1985

                                  The government’s case, in the words of a statute passed while the Meriam
                                  claim was already before the courts.
                                  What they said
                                  The long title was “An Act to allay any doubts that may exist concerning
                                  certain islands forming part of Queensland.” Section 3 declared that, on
                                  annexation, “the islands were vested in the Crown in right of Queensland
   A document mark, not a
 likeness. The witness is the
                                  freed from all other rights, interests and claims of any kind whatsoever and
     State of Queensland,         became waste lands of the Crown.” Section 5 declared: “No compensation
speaking through a 1985 Act       was or is payable to any person” by reason of the annexation, or in respect
        of Parliament.
                                  of any right, interest or claim alleged to have existed before it, or by reason
                                  of any later disposal.
                                  Could they have seen it?
                                  This is not one person’s memory. It is a Parliament changing, or trying to
                                  declare, the legal consequences of annexation in 1879. The High Court in
                                  1988 treated the declarations as an attempt to extinguish the very rights the
                                  Meriam plaintiffs were claiming. A statute can be evidence of a
                                  government’s position. It is not evidence of how the islands were actually
                                  occupied.
                                  Why might they say it?
                                  The Act’s own title said it was to “allay any doubts.” Passed while the
                                  Meriam case was already before the courts, it tried to declare the islands
                                  free of other rights, with no compensation. Students can ask what that
                                  timing shows.
                                  Source. Queensland Coast Islands Declaratory Act 1985 (Qld), assented to 15 April 1985, ss 3
                                  and 5. The High Court later held the Act invalid, to the extent of inconsistency with the Racial
                                  Discrimination Act, in Mabo (No 1) [1988] HCA 69.

My finding
CASE 14 · YEAR 10 · MABO AND TERRA NULLIUS, 1982–1992 · DECIDE

The three witness cards are Eddie Koiki Mabo, Justice Brennan, and the State of Queensland, speaking through the
1985 Act.

There is no answer at the back. The narrator of the notebook is invented. The quoted words, the
1985 Act, and the dates are not. Eddie Mabo did not hear the judgment. Write only what these
records can support. One of the findings you may choose is that we can’t know.

Was Australia ever really treated as ‘nobody’s land’?
Circle one: The law did treat Indigenous land rights as if they were not there · The Latin phrase
terra nullius is a later label, and the earlier official language used other words · The 1985 Act shows
Queensland trying to declare the islands nobody else’s, after the case had begun · We can’t know,
from this file, exactly when the Latin phrase entered Australian legal usage · Another finding, written
below


  MY FINDING
  My finding. ________________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________
  The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
  ______________________________________________________________
  What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________




Why it still matters
The 1992 judgment is still taught as a turning point, and the phrase terra nullius is still argued
over. Families on Mer, and native-title law after 1993, did not end on 3 June 1992. A careful
finding will say what the records show, and what they cannot say for people who were not
asked, or who did not live to hear the result.

Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. This

deceased-persons warning should stay on the student pages.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/mabo-case/#sleuth


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The phrase debate
  Brennan J describes a “fiction” that treated Indigenous land rights as non-existent, and an “enlarged
  notion of terra nullius.” Historians and some lawyers, including David Ritter, have asked when the
  Latin phrase itself was first used in Australian law, and whether earlier official language used other
  words for a similar idea.
  Question. What changes when a later Latin label is treated as if it had been the official slogan of
  1788?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. The 1985 Act, and Mabo (No 1)
  The Queensland Coast Islands Declaratory Act was assented to on 15 April 1985, while the Meriam
  case was already before the courts. In 1988 the High Court held it invalid to the extent it clashed with
  the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.
  Question. Why might a government pass a declaratory Act after a land case has already begun, and
  what did the 1988 decision change?




  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. He never heard the judgment
  Eddie Koiki Mabo died on 21 January 1992. The High Court decided Mabo (No 2) on 3 June 1992.
  This file does not invent what he would have said that day.
  Question. What does a gap like that ask you to do, and what does it ask you not to do?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. What the 1992 orders did, and did not do
The Court recognised native title, and Meriam rights in most of the Murray Islands, subject to some
particular Crown interests. The Native Title Act 1993 followed. This file does not pretend the decision
“gave the land back” in a simple way to all First Nations people, and it does not try the later cases.
Question. What can one judgment settle, and what does it leave open?




STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Fact-finding on Mer
Fact-finding by Moynihan J in the Queensland Supreme Court did not accept all of Eddie Mabo’s
particular claims to individual land. The High Court still recognised Meriam native title in most of
the islands. Both of those things can be true at once.
Question. Why might a court accept a people’s title, and still not accept every individual claim made
in the evidence?

CASE 14 · YEAR 10 · MABO AND TERRA NULLIUS, 1982–1992 · TEACHER

Teacher Note
NOTE


This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page. The user’s name is kept off the student pages and off
the app.


What’s true about the opener
The narrator is an invented Year 10 student. The quoted words, the 1985 Act, and the dates are
not. The close line, “He never heard the judgment,” is this file’s frame for a fact that is not in
dispute: Eddie Mabo died on 21 January 1992; the judgment was 3 June 1992.


Care this case needs
Draft, pending consultation with the Meriam people of Mer, and with AIATSIS guidance. A
deceased-persons warning should stay on the student pages. No photograph of Eddie Koiki
Mabo is used; a silhouette is used instead. No likeness has been invented. Living descendants
are not dated or pictured. Students should not be asked to role-play the judgment, or to invent a
speech for a person who has died.


Curriculum
Australian Curriculum v9, Year 10 History: AC9HH10K10, AC9HH10K11 and AC9HH10K13
(rights and freedoms, the Mabo decision, and the development of native title in the period of
the depth study).


Placement
In this chronological book the case is Case 14, placed by the High Court decision of 3 June 1992.
The writ was filed in May 1982, the same year as the Perth Mint swindle (Case 13). This file is
dated by the judgment, which is the event the typographic page is built around.


Pictures
Eddie Koiki Mabo, Justice Brennan, and the State of Queensland are represented by silhouettes
or a document mark, labelled as such, not likenesses. Official judicial portraits remain in
copyright. No photograph of a deceased Torres Strait Islander person is used in this draft.


Resources
Students can also read the notebook as an interactive book, on a tablet or phone. The page
on screen is the same typographic notebook as the pages in this book. The app is built and
ready; it should be published only when you say go. The QR code uses an island emblem at
the centre.
